CALIFORNIA STATEWIDE JUST CAUSE EVICTION AND RENT CAP (AB 1482) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Properties, LLC · Jordan T. Reyes

INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE
This information sheet describes California's statewide Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (AB 1482), which consists of two related but separate statutory requirements that apply to many, but not all, California residential tenancies: a cap on how much rent may be increased over a 12-month period (Civil Code section 1947.12), and a requirement that a landlord have "just cause," stated in the written termination notice itself, before ending certain tenancies (Civil Code section 1946.2). It concerns the property commonly known as 456 Maple Street, Apt 2, Oakland, CA, the tenancy of Jordan T. Reyes, and the landlord Acme Properties, LLC. If a current monthly rent figure is relevant, it is stated here as: 2,400.

This document is distinct from a specific eviction notice -- such as a three-day notice to pay rent or quit for nonpayment, or a three-day notice to perform covenant or quit for another lease violation -- and describes instead the broader statewide statutory framework of occupancy thresholds, just-cause categories, rent-increase limits, and exemptions within which those specific notices operate. This information sheet does not itself determine whether this or any other specific tenancy is covered by, or exempt from, the statewide rent cap or the statewide just-cause requirement, and it does not calculate the legality of any specific rent increase or termination.

THE 12-MONTH OCCUPANCY THRESHOLD AND WHAT "JUST CAUSE" MEANS
California's Tenant Protection Act sets an occupancy-based threshold before its just-cause requirement attaches to a residential tenancy, and then defines just cause as one of two statutory categories. Once a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months, the landlord may not terminate the tenancy without just cause stated in the written termination notice. If an additional adult tenant is added to the lease before an existing tenant reaches that 12-month mark, the threshold instead requires either that all tenants have occupied the unit for 12 months or more, or that at least one tenant has occupied it for 24 months or more. The statute defines "just cause" as being either "at-fault just cause" or "no-fault just cause," each broken into specific, enumerated grounds addressed in other clauses of this document. As currently enacted, this just-cause requirement is scheduled to expire and be repealed on January 1, 2030.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy. If any additional adult tenants are added to the lease before an existing tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied the residential real property for 24 months, then this subdivision shall only apply if either of the following are satisfied: (1) All of the tenants have continuously and lawfully occupied the residential real property for 12 months or more. (2) One or more tenants have continuously and lawfully occupied the residential real property for 24 months or more."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1946.2(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.2.)

THE ENUMERATED "AT-FAULT" JUST-CAUSE GROUNDS
Civil Code section 1946.2(b)(1) lists eleven specific grounds that qualify as "at-fault just cause" for terminating a tenancy that has crossed the occupancy threshold. Four of them are quoted below: default in the payment of rent; a breach of a material term of the lease (the same kind of breach addressed by Code of Civil Procedure section 1161(3)), including violating a lease provision after a written notice to correct it; maintaining or permitting a nuisance; and committing waste. The statute separately lists (among others) a tenant's refusal, after written demand, to sign a renewal or extension lease of similar duration and terms; criminal activity by the tenant on the property, or criminal activity or a criminal threat directed at the owner or the owner's agent; an unauthorized assignment or sublease; refusing to allow the owner lawful entry; using the premises for an unlawful purpose; an employee, agent, or licensee's failure to vacate after that relationship ends; and a tenant's failure to deliver possession after the tenant's own notice of intent to terminate, or an accepted written offer to surrender. For a curable lease violation, the statute separately requires the landlord to first give the tenant a notice of the violation with an opportunity to cure -- specifically cross-referenced to Code of Civil Procedure section 1161(3) -- before a termination notice for that violation may be served.

(C) Maintaining, committing, or permitting the maintenance or commission of a nuisance as described in paragraph (4) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (D) Committing waste as described in paragraph (4) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure."

THE ENUMERATED "NO-FAULT" JUST-CAUSE GROUNDS
Civil Code section 1946.2(b)(2) lists four grounds that qualify as "no-fault just cause" -- reasons for ending a tenancy that do not depend on anything the tenant did. They are: (1) intent to occupy the property, for at least 12 continuous months as a primary residence, by the owner or the owner's spouse, domestic partner, child, grandchild, parent, or grandparent, subject to detailed conditions on timing, required notice content, and what happens if the intended occupant does not actually move in; (2) withdrawal of the property from the rental market; (3) the owner's compliance with a government agency or court order relating to habitability, a government agency or court order to vacate, or a local ordinance that necessitates vacating; and (4) intent to demolish, or to substantially remodel, the property, where "substantially remodel" is itself statutorily defined and requires the tenant to vacate for at least 30 consecutive days, and a termination notice on this ground must include a specific statutory statement about the tenant's right to re-rent the unit if the remodel or demolition is not carried out. Each no-fault ground listed above triggers the relocation-assistance-or-rent-waiver requirement described in a separate clause of this document.

RELOCATION ASSISTANCE OR A RENT WAIVER REQUIRED FOR NO-FAULT TERMINATIONS
When a landlord terminates a covered tenancy for one of the no-fault just-cause grounds described elsewhere in this document, Civil Code section 1946.2(d) requires the landlord -- regardless of the tenant's income, and at the landlord's own election -- to do one of two things: either pay the tenant direct relocation assistance, or waive in writing the rent for the final month of the tenancy before that rent becomes due. The amount, whichever form is chosen, is set by statute as equal to one month of the tenant's rent in effect when the termination notice was issued, and if relocation assistance is paid rather than the rent waived, it must be paid within 15 calendar days of the notice being served. The statute states expressly that a landlord's failure to strictly comply with this relocation-assistance-or-rent-waiver requirement renders the termination notice void.

(B) Waive in writing the payment of rent for the final month of the tenancy, prior to the rent becoming due."

THE STATEWIDE RENT-INCREASE CAP FORMULA
Civil Code section 1947.12(a) caps how much a covered landlord may increase rent over any 12-month period. The cap is 5 percent plus the percentage change in the applicable regional consumer price index, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, applied to the lowest gross rental rate charged for the unit at any time during the 12 months before the increase takes effect (with any rent discounts, incentives, or concessions offered and accepted excluded from that baseline figure). If the same tenant remains in the unit over a 12-month period, the rent may not be increased more than twice within that period, even if each individual increase would otherwise fit within the percentage cap. The "percentage change in the cost of living" figure used in the formula is tied to the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers for a specific metropolitan area (or a statewide substitute where no regional index exists), not a single statewide number. The cap applies only to increases on an existing tenancy: for a new tenancy in which no tenant from the prior tenancy remains in lawful possession, the landlord may set the initial rental rate without regard to this cap, and the cap applies again only to increases after that initial rate is set. If a current monthly rent figure for this tenancy is relevant, it is stated here as: 2,400.

EXEMPTIONS FROM THE STATEWIDE RENT CAP
Civil Code section 1947.12(d) lists six categories of residential real property to which the statewide rent cap does not apply. They are: (1) housing that is deed-restricted, or otherwise subject to a recorded document or government agreement, as affordable housing for very low, low, or moderate income persons and families; (2) dormitories owned and operated by a college, university, or K-12 school; (3) housing already subject to a local rent- or price-control ordinance that restricts annual increases to an amount less than this statute's own cap; (4) housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, unless it is a mobilehome; (5) certain residential property alienable separate from any other dwelling unit, subject to non-corporate-ownership conditions and a required exemption notice described in a separate clause of this document; and (6) a two-unit property in which the owner occupies one unit as a principal residence, so long as the owner continues to occupy it and neither unit is an accessory dwelling unit.

EXEMPTIONS FROM THE STATEWIDE JUST-CAUSE REQUIREMENT
Civil Code section 1946.2(e) lists nine categories of residential real property or residential circumstances to which the statewide just-cause requirement does not apply. Among them: transient and tourist hotel occupancy; housing in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended care facility, or licensed elder- or adult-care facility; dormitories owned and operated by a college, university, or K-12 school; housing where the tenant shares a bathroom or kitchen with an owner who maintains a principal residence there; a single-family owner-occupied residence in which the owner-occupant rents or leases no more than two units or bedrooms; a two-unit property where the owner occupies one unit as a principal residence; housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, unless it is a mobilehome; certain property alienable separate from any other dwelling unit, subject to non-corporate-ownership conditions and a required exemption notice addressed in a separate clause of this document; and housing that is deed-restricted, or otherwise subject to a recorded document or government agreement, as affordable housing for very low, low, or moderate income persons and families. This statewide just-cause requirement is also displaced, rather than layered on top of, certain local just-cause ordinances: a property already subject to a local just-cause ordinance adopted on or before September 1, 2019, is governed by that local ordinance instead, and a property subject to a local just-cause ordinance adopted or amended after that date is likewise governed by the local ordinance instead of this section, but only if the local ordinance meets the statute's own definition of "more protective."

This document is distinct from a specific eviction notice -- such as a three-day notice to pay rent or quit for nonpayment, or a three-day notice to perform covenant or quit for another lease violation -- and describes instead the broader statewide statutory framework of occupancy thresholds, just-cause categories, rent-increase limits, and exemptions within which those specific notices operate. California's Tenant Protection Act sets an occupancy-based threshold before its just-cause requirement attaches to a residential tenancy, and then defines just cause as one of two statutory categories. Once a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months, the landlord may not terminate the tenancy without just cause stated in the written termination notice. If an additional adult tenant is added to the lease before an existing tenant reaches that 12-month mark, the threshold instead requires either that all tenants have occupied the unit for 12 months or more, or that at least one tenant has occupied it for 24 months or more. The statute defines "just cause" as being either "at-fault just cause" or "no-fault just cause," each broken into specific, enumerated grounds addressed in other clauses of this document. As currently enacted, this just-cause requirement is scheduled to expire and be repealed on January 1, 2030.

The cap is 5 percent plus the percentage change in the applicable regional consumer price index, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, applied to the lowest gross rental rate charged for the unit at any time during the 12 months before the increase takes effect (with any rent discounts, incentives, or concessions offered and accepted excluded from that baseline figure). The cap applies only to increases on an existing tenancy: for a new tenancy in which no tenant from the prior tenancy remains in lawful possession, the landlord may set the initial rental rate without regard to this cap, and the cap applies again only to increases after that initial rate is set.
